title: South Asians Have the Highest Heart Disease Risk at 45 — Despite Eating Better and Drinking Less Than Everyone Else
excerpt: A decade-long study of 2,700 U.S. adults found that South Asian men and women develop prediabetes, hypertension, and high cholesterol earlier than every other racial group — even though they report healthier diets and lower alcohol use. The researchers say visceral fat and early-life exposures may explain the paradox.
body:
One of the largest longitudinal studies of South Asian cardiovascular health in the United States has landed on a finding that is as unsettling as it is important: by age 45, South Asian adults already carry the highest burden of heart disease risk factors of any racial or ethnic group in the country — even though they report eating better, drinking less, and exercising about as much as their peers.

The study, led by researchers at Northwestern Medicine and published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, combined data from two long-running cohort studies — MASALA (Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America) and MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) — to track how cardiovascular risk factors evolve between ages 45 and 55 across South Asian, white, Black, Hispanic, and Chinese adults.

## The Numbers Are Stark

At age 45, nearly one in three South Asian men (31%) already had prediabetes — a rate that dwarfs every other group. Among white men, the figure was just 4%. Black and Hispanic men were at 10%, and Chinese men at 13%.

Hypertension told a similar story. One in four South Asian men had high blood pressure by 45, compared to 18% of white men, 10% of Hispanic men, and just 6% of Chinese men. South Asian men also had higher rates of dyslipidemia — elevated cholesterol or triglycerides — than Black men (78% vs. 61%).

South Asian women followed the same pattern. By age 45, roughly 18% had prediabetes, about twice the rate seen in white, Black, Hispanic, and Chinese women.

By age 55, South Asian adults were at least twice as likely to have developed diabetes as white adults.

## The Paradox

What makes these numbers so striking is the context. South Asian participants in MASALA reported healthier diets, lower alcohol use, comparable physical activity levels, and lower average BMI than most other groups in the study.

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviors and clinical risk was surprising," said Dr. Namratha Kandula, professor of general internal medicine and epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and the study's senior author. "This paradox tells us we're missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians."

## Where the Risk May Be Hiding

Kandula and her team point to several factors that conventional screening may miss.

First, visceral fat. Prior MASALA data show that South Asians accumulate more fat around their organs — liver, heart, abdomen — than other groups, even at a normal or low BMI. Other research has shown this pattern begins in childhood. Visceral fat is far more metabolically active than subcutaneous fat, driving insulin resistance, inflammation, and arterial damage in ways that BMI alone does not capture.

Second, early-life exposures. Most MASALA participants are immigrants whose childhood nutrition, environmental stressors, and activity patterns in South Asia may have programmed cardiometabolic risk long before they adopted healthier habits in the U.S.

Third, genetics. South Asians account for roughly one-quarter of the world's population but bear an estimated 60% of the global burden of heart disease. They develop atherosclerosis — the buildup of plaque in arteries that leads to heart attacks — up to a decade earlier than the general population on average.

## What the Diaspora Should Know

For the estimated 5.4 million South Asians living in the United States, the clinical takeaway is blunt: do not wait until midlife to screen for heart disease.

"Clinicians should start looking for high blood sugar, high blood pressure, and other risk-enhancing factors, such as lipoprotein(a), before midlife," Kandula said. She also stressed the need for "culturally appropriate lifestyle counseling to help South Asians eat healthy, exercise regularly, and minimize tobacco and alcohol."

For individuals, Kandula's advice is equally direct: "Even if you eat well and exercise, you may still be at higher risk for diabetes and high blood pressure at younger ages. Ask your doctor about early screening — and get your blood pressure, fasting glucose or A1c, cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) checked before middle age, because early detection, treatment, and control of these risk factors can prevent heart disease."

Chandrika Gopal, a 58-year-old MASALA participant from Ohio who was born in southern India, said the study changed how she thinks about her own health. "Even if we eat well, we can still be at higher risk," she said. "Living in a new country, adapting to different food and routines — it all adds up."

## The Bigger Picture

The study arrives alongside a new clinical practice statement from the American Society for Preventive Cardiology, published in the American Journal of Preventive Cardiology, that lays out a comprehensive framework for managing cardiometabolic risk in South Asians — from individual screening and culturally tailored clinics to community-level assessments of social determinants and acculturation.

For a diaspora community that is among the fastest-growing and highest-earning demographic groups in the U.S., the message is clear: prosperity and healthy habits are not enough to outrun a biological predisposition that may be set in motion long before immigration. Early screening, targeted interventions, and a willingness to look beyond BMI may be the most important investments South Asian Americans can make in their own longevity.

*Sources: Journal of the American Heart Association (MASALA/MESA study), Northwestern Medicine, American Journal of Preventive Cardiology (ASPC clinical practice statement)*
